Foot Puncture Infection: Name the Organism from the Exposure and the Clock

A nail through a shoe and a foot still sore weeks later is Pseudomonas

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

After a foot puncture, the exposure and the clock name the organism:

  • First 1 to 4 days, spreading redness: cellulitis from Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci.
  • Nail through a shoe, pain and redness persisting a week or more, little fever, often a normal WBC (white blood cell count): osteomyelitis or osteochondritis (bone or cartilage infection) from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, carried in from the shoe's foam sole.
  • Wound soaked in fresh water at injury (NBME adds soil), then a fast-spreading infection: Aeromonas hydrophila. Salt water: Vibrio vulnificus.

A normal film does not exclude bone infection; MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) does better. Treat with debridement and bone culture, covering Pseudomonas and S. aureus.

Diagnosis
How NBME framed it: question 1

7-year-old boy, follow-up 3 weeks after a nail went through his shoe into the right foot wound thoroughly cleaned and bandaged; moderate pain persists tetanus vaccine at age 5; otherwise healthy Red, warm skin over the wound, tender to touch T 37.2 °C · other vital signs normal

Most likely causal organism?

Competing answers
  • Aeromonas hydrophila: a wound pathogen that also causes diarrhea and infections in immunocompromised hosts; but it needs fresh water or soil in the wound at injury; this stem gives a shoe and a 3-week course.
  • Group A streptococcus: causes cellulitis; but as a fast-spreading skin infection in the first days, not a deep infection weeks after a puncture.
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae: a gram-negative rod like the key; but it causes aspiration pneumonia, not puncture-wound bone infection.
  • Staphylococcus aureus: the most common cause of osteomyelitis; but a nail through a shoe with a deep infection weeks later points to Pseudomonas.

Down to two: Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus. Pseudomonas aeruginosa: a nail through a shoe, then pain, redness and warmth still present at 3 weeks with a near-normal temperature, is osteomyelitis by direct inoculation. The stem never names osteomyelitis. NBME calls Pseudomonas the puncture-wound organism; that holds for the deep infection weeks after a shoe puncture, while the first days are S. aureus or streptococci. Tetanus at age 5 is 2 years ago: no booster, and no organism.

Management and treatment
By situation Osteomyelitis – surgical debridement, bone cultures, empiric antibiotics covering Pseudomonas and S. aureus · Through a shoe – past 72 hours with signs of infection, add Pseudomonas coverage · Tetanus – a puncture is tetanus-prone: booster if the last dose was over 5 years ago; it names no organism · Fever – a near-normal temperature does not argue against bone infection after a puncture
Practice
  1. 10-year-old boy, 10 days after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel improved at first; heel pain now returning limps; mild swelling and tenderness No water exposure Afebrile · WBC normal · MRI: calcaneal marrow edema → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → a deep infection 1 to 2 weeks after a nail through a sneaker, often afebrile with a normal white count, is Pseudomonas osteomyelitis; S. aureus and streptococci cause the early cellulitis
  2. 9-year-old girl stepped barefoot on a tack on the kitchen floor 2 days ago spreading redness around the puncture warm and tender No water or soil exposure T 38.1 °C · foot radiograph normal → Staphylococcus aureus → a puncture infection in the first days is cellulitis, most often Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci; through a sneaker, a deep infection that appears 1 to 2 weeks later points to Pseudomonas
  3. 15-year-old boy cut his sole on a branch while wading barefoot in a lake 1 day later: rapidly spreading painful redness foot swollen Fresh water, not the sea T 38.9 °C · HR 112/min → Aeromonas hydrophila → a fast-spreading wound infection soon after fresh-water exposure is Aeromonas hydrophila; salt water or raw shellfish points to Vibrio vulnificus
  4. 8-year-old boy, 2 weeks after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel worsening heel pain and swelling tender over the calcaneus Walks on his toes T 37.4 °C · foot radiographs normal → MRI of the foot → early radiographs are often normal in osteomyelitis; MRI is more sensitive and shows marrow edema
  5. 11-year-old girl was diagnosed with calcaneal osteomyelitis by MRI today a nail went through her sneaker 3 weeks ago heel pain and swelling persist Afebrile and otherwise well T 37.3 °C · foot film normal → Surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics → osteomyelitis after a puncture through a shoe needs surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics, plus S. aureus coverage until cultures return
Pairs with The Limping Child: Sick or Well, Then Age and Time: a limp after a nail through a shoe routes here. Septic Arthritis in a Child: Aspirate, or Treat and Recheck?: joint organisms by host. Diabetic Foot Ulcer: diabetes also carries a high risk of Pseudomonas osteomyelitis.
Transferable rule

Name the organism from the exposure and the clock: a shoe and weeks mean Pseudomonas; the first days mean S. aureus or streptococci.
